title: Story Protocol: Building a Modern IP Infrastructure and Protecting Creators in the AI Age (Andrea Muttoni - President Story Foundation)
author: Andrea Muttoni

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source does not assess legal task redesign, user expertise or verification. It instead relocates the decisive constraint upstream, emphasizing access to high-quality, legally cleared real-world training data and licensing infrastructure rather than selective deployment within legal workflows.
qs: And the reason being is a model is only as good as the data that it can ingest.
It's IP safe, IP cleared real world data, right?

st.t: Pragmatic adoption: Experimentation outruns transformation evidence
st.an: Muttoni’s recommendation exemplifies pragmatic, hands-on experimentation while providing no measured usability, legal-effect or AI-related outcome evidence. It therefore supports the cluster’s distinction between encouraging trials and demonstrating transformation.
qs: So I would highly encourage everyone to go to the portal and register any image that they have lying around or any drawing just to see how easy the experience is.

kp.k: Blockchain infrastructure supplements rather than replaces IP law
kp.d: Story Foundation president Andrea Muttoni presents Story as an infrastructure layer intended to simplify participation in IP registration, licensing, attribution and remixing as AI accelerates content production. He contrasts this ambition with the expense and complexity commonly associated with IP processes; these are the provider's rationale and objectives, not demonstrated outcomes.
qs: We're not trying to replace the legal system, we're just trying to add a layer on top of it to make it more liquid, to make it easy to participate for everyone, and to make it easy for IP to be used and remixed and rightfully attributed across the internet because the internet is exploding in content, especially with AI now, right?

kp.k: Immutable registration supplies evidence of creation
kp.d: Muttoni distinguishes a defensive registration function from proactive licensing and monetization. He argues that recording IP on an immutable ledger supplies additional evidence of creation, while stating that copyright does not depend on Copyright Office registration. The discussion presents his account of evidentiary value, rather than a judicial finding about blockchain records.
qs: One is the defensive aspect, which is I want to register it so that I can prove that I created it before someone else, right?
And so when you register it on Story, you're giving yourself more proof, more evidence, more security around, okay, this was what I created and here's how I can prove it.

kp.k: Configurable licenses aim to reduce bespoke legal transactions
kp.d: Muttoni says Story developed its programmable IP license (PIL) with a large legal firm. Rights holders can configure commercial use, attribution and licensing charges, and users can obtain licenses directly rather than arranging meetings and introductions. He presents this as simplifying lawful reuse without requiring owners to be lawyers, but provides no measured reduction in legal costs or lawyer workload.
qs: We worked with a very big legal firm to develop the programmable IP license, which we call the PIL, P-I-L.
So you don't need to be a lawyer to personalize your license, right?
They can just go to your IP and read the license terms and just click get a license and they can get a license.

kp.k: Machine-readable terms enable automated dataset licensing
kp.d: Muttoni describes smart contracts that allow applications to query licensing conditions without reading PDFs and automatically license qualifying assets. His example is selecting images for AI datasets according to acceptable terms and prices. This is a proposed mechanism for automating rights transactions, not evidence that AI independently resolves legal interpretation.
qs: So you could create code logic that evaluates certain IPs based on license terms that you can programmatically query without having to open a PDF and read it, which is very powerful.

So you can, for example, you could write a tool that scrolls through all different types of IPs on Story and automatically licenses any IP within a certain category that you want that satisfies the terms and conditions that you need, right?

kp.k: Programmable licenses connect on-chain transactions to legal documents
kp.d: Using the analogy of converting dollars into and out of USDC, Muttoni describes bringing legal terms on-chain and converting customized licenses back into paper documents. He asserts that the PIL is usable outside the blockchain to defend IP; the transcript supplies no litigation or enforcement results validating that assertion.
qs: Because the PIL is a license that is viable in the real world.
And so whenever you want to off-ramp this programmable license, you can always rasterize it back to a paper document that contains all of your personalizations, all of your custom parameters.
And that is a license that you can go and use to defend your IP wherever you need, right?

kp.k: AI training disputes expose unequal creator enforcement capacity
kp.d: Muttoni asserts that large models have ingested internet content and contrasts litigation by organizations such as the New York Times and Reddit with independent creators' limited ability to respond. He discusses style imitation as a creator concern but explicitly declines to explore the fair-use debate in depth. These are his characterizations of the market and disputes, not adjudicated conclusions about infringement.
qs: And I know that right now we're in the very middle of a fair use debacle where I don't want to get too much into that side of the debate, but we are in a gold rush time when it comes to data, right?

And so that's why they're facing several lawsuits with the companies that are big enough to take them on, like the New York Times, like Reddit, and independent creators are kind of left stranded, right?

kp.k: Poseidon targets scarce real-world AI training data
kp.d: Muttoni argues that models and compute have largely commoditized, making data the scarce frontier. He positions the newly announced Poseidon platform around sourcing videos of tasks, sensor readings and speech for applications including robotics and autonomous driving. Licensing and IP registration would occur on Story. This is a strategic market thesis and early-stage product proposition, not comparative performance evidence.
qs: Poseidon is a Web 3 take on that, which is models and compute have pretty much become commoditized.
So the real third frontier that has not been commoditized yet is data.
real world data that is used to train real world models like robotics, like autonomous driving.
And all of this licensing and registration of this IP, of this data IP, will happen on Story, right?

kp.k: Dataset contributors should receive attribution and recurring compensation
kp.d: Muttoni distinguishes facts and numbers from the work of collecting, cleaning, annotating and preparing datasets, which he characterizes as IP. He argues that all contributors should receive attribution and payment whenever a dataset is used. This is his legal characterization and compensation objective, rather than evidence that every dataset is protected or payments already occur.
qs: Like, facts and numbers are not really IP, but the collection and the processing and the cleaning up and the annotating and the preparing of all of that information into a data set is definitely IP, right?
And everyone who contributed to that data set should be able to not only be attributed but also receive compensation anytime that data set is used.

kp.k: Token incentives could replace some manual data procurement
kp.d: Muttoni proposes that points or tokens could coordinate worldwide contributions in response to data needs or proactively, reducing reliance on individually negotiated procurement arrangements. He explicitly labels his description of how Scale AI might procure data as speculation. He also qualifies Poseidon's maturity: it is in very early stages and talking to large AI companies, rather than reporting completed adoption or established network effects.
qs: And so how someone like Scale AI would work is, and this is speculation at this point,
anyone can contribute their data and receive, whether it's points or tokens in return, right?
Now, one caveat is Poseidon is still very, very early days, but we're already talking to some very big AI companies.

kp.k: Rights clearance is positioned as an AI buyer incentive
kp.d: Muttoni argues that AI companies increasingly want assurance that training data will not generate later legal problems. He presents end-to-end attribution and licensing through Story as Poseidon's differentiator from internet datasets whose users rely on fair-use claims. His assertion of IP clearance is a product proposition, without documented clearance procedures or legal outcomes in the transcript.
qs: It's not just real world data. It's IP safe, IP cleared real world data, right?
They need to be sure that the data that they use for models won't come and bite them in the butt later on.
the final data set can be attributed and IP cleared from start to finish

kp.d: Muttoni explains that Story stores IP metadata and license terms, not the underlying files. He agrees with the host's envisioned workflow in which acceptance and payment lead to data access, and describes restricting externally stored files to license holders as built-in enforcement. The mechanism concerns access control rather than a claim that blockchain controls all subsequent use.
qs: All of the IP-related metadata is stored on Story. So what is this IP? What are the licensing terms? All of that is all on Story. But the underlying file is not.
So for example, only people who have a license can get access to that file, right? That creates some enforcement built in.

kp.k: Specialized infrastructure handles interdependent licensing and royalty obligations
kp.d: Muttoni says Story's proof-of-creativity protocol covers registration, licensing, royalty flows and disputes. He attributes the decision to build a dedicated base-layer blockchain to hierarchical, graph-like relationships among IP assets: transactions must check related rights and royalties. He reports unsuccessful suitability assessments of other chains and a layer-two approach, but supplies no comparative benchmarks.
qs: The whole proof of creativity protocol that regulates not only the licensing but the royalty rails, the disputes, all of the logic behind dealing and registering and licensing IP is all thanks to this proof of creativity protocol, which the story L1 was built around.

because every transaction needs to check every parent, basically every other IP that has any form of relationship with the IP that you're trying to transact on and do all the licensing checks and do all the royalty checks before any transaction can occur.

kp.k: Roadmap extends licensing to composite datasets and privacy
kp.d: For the next six months, Muttoni describes planned Poseidon work on data pipelines, cleaning and automatic labeling, alongside Story protocol expansion to support the programmable data license and datasets assembled from multiple contributions. He also signals prospective interoperability and privacy innovations intended to preserve permissionless licensing. These are development plans, not completed capabilities.
qs: So taking out moments that are not useful, automatically labeling certain actions, all of that needs to happen before a piece of data is actually useful for an A company to use.
So that means expanding the proof of creativity protocol to, for example, support the programmable data license, to introduce new forms of IP that are related to AI training and data sets.
really novel ways to create this secrecy and privacy around IP without sacrificing the permissionlessness of the licensing and the participation that a blockchain enables.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Andrea Muttoni argues that AI-driven content growth creates a need for more accessible IP registration, licensing and attribution infrastructure.
pts.d: Muttoni presents Story as a layer over the existing legal system, not a replacement. He says blockchain registration provides evidence of creation, while its customizable programmable IP license lets nonlawyers set commercial-use, attribution and payment terms and lets users acquire licenses without introductions or meetings. He further claims that machine-readable terms enable automated selection and licensing of material for AI datasets, and that the programmable license can be converted into a paper document for real-world use. These are descriptions of capabilities and intended benefits, not claims about measured reductions in legal employment or spending.

pts.k: Muttoni identifies specialized real-world training data as AI's next scarce resource and a new licensing market.
pts.d: He argues that models and compute have largely commoditized, while internet data has already been ingested. He therefore positions private or newly generated real-world data—video of tasks, sensor readings and speech—as the next frontier, especially for robotics and autonomous driving. Poseidon is intended to source this data and use Story for registration and licensing. His broad assertions about commoditization and internet ingestion are his market assessment, not findings established by a study in the interview.

pts.k: Muttoni predicts that programmable incentives and licensing can coordinate distributed data contributors and compensate them for AI training inputs.
pts.d: He contrasts token- or points-based participation with manually negotiated procurement and subcontracting. He explicitly labels his account of Scale AI's procurement process as speculation. His proposed model enables contributors worldwide to supply requested data or contribute proactively. Compensation whenever a dataset is used is expressed as a normative goal, not a demonstrated payment outcome. He distinguishes facts and numbers from the collection, processing and annotation of datasets, which he characterizes as IP.

pts.k: Muttoni says AI-training litigation increases demand for rights-cleared data, and presents end-to-end licensing and access controls as a response.
pts.d: He claims that large rights holders can pursue AI companies while independent creators are left without comparable recourse. He argues that AI companies increasingly want assurance against future IP disputes and that contributor-level licensing can produce attributed, rights-cleared datasets. Story stores IP metadata and licensing terms, not the underlying files; external file access can be restricted to license holders. He describes this as partial built-in enforcement, rather than a replacement for courts, and declines to resolve the fair-use debate.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered is principally Muttoni's firsthand product account and market interpretation, supplemented by external examples and an authority reference.
pts.d: As Story Foundation president, Muttoni describes license development with an unnamed large law firm, smart-contract functionality and the publicly accessible IP portal. He cites a WIPO estimate of $80 trillion in intangible assets as market context, not as evidence of AI-specific demand or Story's effectiveness. He invokes Facebook's reported $14 billion investment in Scale AI to illustrate demand for data, mentions New York Times and Reddit litigation, and refers to allegations that Facebook torrented books. He also reports discussions with unnamed large AI companies. The interview supplies no adoption counts, realized contributor earnings, legal-cost comparisons, benchmarks or adjudicated validation of the licensing model.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The 2025 interview distinguishes existing Story functionality from an early-stage Poseidon initiative and a roughly six-month development roadmap.
pts.d: Muttoni describes Story's registration and configurable licensing as presently available. Poseidon is at the announcement and fundraising stage; company discussions, even those described as advanced, are not presented as completed customer deployments. Over the next six months he anticipates building data-pipeline applications, cleaning and labeling capabilities, support for the programmable data license and additional interoperability and privacy features. Benefits depend on obtaining suitable data, making it useful for training, implementing licensing and access arrangements, and attracting contributors and buyers. He provides no firm date or quantified forecast for broad adoption.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected groups are creators, data contributors and owners, AI developers and IP-infrastructure builders; effects on the legal profession are indirect.
pts.d: For artists and other rights holders, Muttoni promises easier registration, licensing, attribution and monetization, with particular concern for independent creators whose work has been used in training. For individuals contributing real-world recordings or dataset preparation, he envisages participation incentives and compensation. For AI companies, especially robotics and autonomous-driving developers, he promises access to specialized, traceably licensed training data. For application developers, he describes infrastructure for querying terms and automating licenses. His suggestion that users need not be lawyers to personalize licenses implies less reliance on bespoke legal interactions for those transactions, but he does not predict lawyer displacement, staffing changes or a quantified impact on legal-service revenues.
